answer.rationale: Timing is the strongest signal available: the release landed ~2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing ~90m ago, which is consistent with a post-deploy regression surfacing under load. But it is genuinely confounded — settlement traffic is simultaneously at daily peak with heavy writes, so rising write latency could be pure load rather than the build. Rollback is the only candidate that addresses the release hypothesis; failover moves load without fixing a bad build, capacity takes longer than the window and treats only the load hypothesis, circuit breakers on the payments dependency do not protect the write path (and failing fast risks exactly the customer writes we must not lose), and read-replica routing addresses dashboard/report load, not settlement writes. I verify memory_b1 because it is the single memory my intended action rests on, and its summary is exactly where I most need the original record: 'the prior build was stable and the rollback finished without customer impact' was learned on day 18 under unknown traffic conditions. Whether that rollback happened during a quiet period or at write peak, and whether the intervening builds introduced schema or data-format changes that make the prior build non-reversible, decides whether rollback here is safe or whether it strands in-flight settlement writes. I do not verify memory_b3 or b2 because even if confirmed they point at interventions that cannot land inside this window. Scale is deliberately a small guarded test rather than a full fleet rollback: memory_b6 shows canary cohorts here surface regressions within an hour, so rolling back a bounded cohort of write traffic lets the release-vs-load question answer itself — if cohort p99 recovers while the rest stays elevated, the release is the cause and full rollback is justified next window; if both stay elevated, it is load and I have not spent my one intervention on the wrong hypothesis. Key risk I am holding open: a peak-traffic rollback can drop or corrupt in-flight settlement writes if the prior build cannot read current-format data, which would violate the primary objective more severely than the latency itself. I proceed only with write draining and a forward-compatibility check on the cohort, and I treat all six inherited summaries as unverified compressions of single past incidents, not as base rates.
